DETAILED ACTION
Notice of Pre-AIA  or AIA  Status
The present application, filed on or after March 16, 2013, is being examined under the first inventor to file provisions of the AIA .
Priority
Receipt is acknowledged of certified copies of papers required by 37 CFR 1.55.
Claim Objections
Claim 7 is objected to because of the following informalities: The limitation “wherein the decorative shell and light head enclosing the colloid encapsulating the first LED chip” in lines 9-10 of the claim is grammatically incorrect. The Examiner respectfully suggests amending it to be --wherein the decorative shell and light head enclose .  Appropriate correction is required.
Claim Rejections - 35 USC § 112
The following is a quotation of 35 U.S.C. 112(b):
(b)  CONCLUSION.—The specification shall conclude with one or more claims particularly pointing out and distinctly claiming the subject matter which the inventor or a joint inventor regards as the invention.
The following is a quotation of 35 U.S.C. 112 (pre-AIA ), second paragraph:
The specification shall conclude with one or more claims particularly pointing out and distinctly claiming the subject matter which the applicant regards as his invention.
Claims 6-12 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) or 35 U.S.C. 112 (pre-AIA ), second paragraph, as being indefinite for failing to particularly point out and distinctly claim the subject matter which the inventor or a joint inventor (or for applications subject to pre-AIA  35 U.S.C. 112, the applicant), regards as the invention.
Claim 6 is rejected as being indefinite as it is not clear if the recitation “wherein the decorative shell is in the shape of one of a mini light bulb, round globe, snowflake, and pentagram” requires the claimed decorative shell to include a shape of at least one of a mini light bulb, round globe, snowflake, and pentagram, or simply at least one of either the shape of a mini light bulb, round globe, snowflake, or pentagram.  The Applicant is respectfully advised that the use of the phrase “at least one of… and…” (or the similar phrase “one or more of… and…”) is a conjunctive list requiring at least one of each of the listed elements; “at least one of… or…” (or the similar phrase “one or more of… or…”) must be used when the intended requirement is to define a structure having at least just one of the cited elements. See Superguide Corp. v DirecTV Enters., Inc., 358 F.3d 870 (69 UPQ2d 1865) (fed. Cir. 2004).  The Applicant is further advised that, in comparing the claimed invention with the Prior Art, the Examiner assumed, based on the originally filed description and drawings, Claim 6 as defining the decorative shell including a shape of at least one of either a mini light bulb, round globe, snowflake, or pentagram.
Regarding claim 7, the limitation “stripped of insulation to expose a portion of the copper strands of each of the first and second wire” in lines 3-4 of the claim renders the claim indefinite because it is unclear what specific structure is being stripped of insulation in this method step, rendering the exact scope of the claim unascertainable. Further, the recitation “the copper strands” lacks antecedent basis. Based on a review of the Specification and Drawings as filed, for the purpose of examination, the Examiner has assumed that this method step requires ends of each of the first and second wire to be stripped of insulation to expose a portion of copper strands inside the first and second wires, and so the Examiner respectfully suggests amending it to be --stripping an end of each of the first wire and the second wire
Claims 8-10 and 12 are rejected due to their dependence on indefinite Claim 7.
Claim 11 is rejected as being indefinite as it is not clear if the recitation “wherein the colloid is formed over the first LED chip using one of injection molding, casting, and foam injection” in lines 1-2 of the claim requires the claimed colloid to be formed by at least one of injecting molding, casting, and foam molding, or simply at least one of either injection molding, casting, or foam molding.  The Applicant is respectfully advised that the use of the phrase “at least one of… and…” (or the similar phrase “one or more of… and…”) is a conjunctive list requiring at least one of each of the listed elements; “at least one of… or…” (or the similar phrase “one or more of… or…”) must be used when the intended requirement is to define a structure having at least just one of the cited elements. See Superguide Corp. v DirecTV Enters., Inc., 358 F.3d 870 (69 UPQ2d 1865) (fed. Cir. 2004).  The Applicant is further advised that, in comparing the claimed invention with the Prior Art, the Examiner assumed, based on the originally filed description and drawings, Claim 11 as defining a method including the colloid being formed using at least one of either foam molding, casting, or foam injection.
Appropriate correction is required.
Claim Rejections - 35 USC § 103
The following is a quotation of 35 U.S.C. 103 which forms the basis for all obviousness rejections set forth in this Office action:
A patent for a claimed invention may not be obtained, notwithstanding that the claimed invention is not identically disclosed as set forth in section 102, if the differences between the claimed invention and the prior art are such that the claimed invention as a whole would have been obvious before the effective filing date of the claimed invention to a person having ordinary skill in the art to which the claimed invention pertains. Patentability shall not be negated by the manner in which the invention was made.
Claims 1-12 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being unpatentable over Tsai (US 12,085,244) in view of Chen (US 2018/0187840).
Regarding claim 1, Tsai teaches a light assembly of a string light (light assembly 100 of a light string 120 of connected light assemblies; see Figs. 1A-9; Abstract; col. 4, lines 23-60; col. 6, lines 50-56; col. 7, lines 8-20, 45-57; col. 15, lines 58-67; col. 16, lines 1-35) comprising a first wire and a second wire, each of the first wire and the second wire comprising an end exposing strands (first conductive lead wire 112 and second conductive lead wire 114 each have exposed conductors at their ends; see Figs. 1A-1F, 2, 8-9; col. 6, lines 50-67; col. 7, lines 1-65); a first light-emitting diode (LED) chip soldered to the exposed strands of the first wire and the second wire (a light emitting source 110 which comprises a light emitter 110C in the form of an LED is soldered to the exposed conductive strands of the first wire 112 and the second wire 114; see Figs. 1A-1F, 2, 8-9; col. 6, lines 50-67; col. 7, lines 1-65; col. 10, lines 20-50); an epoxy resin encapsulating the first LED chip soldered to the first wire and the second wire (a filler 116 such as epoxy resin or similar material is deposited in a light cap 104 and positioned over the first LED 110 to encapsulate the LED and its solder connections to the first and second wires 112, 114; see Figs. 1A-1F, 2; 8-9; col. 7, lines 66-67; col. 8, lines 1-47; col. 10, lines 12-58); a light head securing the epoxy resin and a part of the first wire and the second wire (housing 106; see Figs. 1A-6C, 8-9; col. 4, lines 47-52; col. 5, lines 36-67; col. 6, lines 13-56; col. 7, lines 8-31, 66-67; col. 8, lines 1-40, 63-67; col. 10, lines 12-67); and a decorative shell secured onto the light head and enclosing the epoxy resin encapsulating the first LED chip (light cap 104 is secured onto the light head 106 and encloses the epoxy resin 116 encapsulating the first LED chip 110 therein; see Figs. 1A-1F, 2, 8-9; col. 4, lines 47-67; col. 5, lines 1-35, 59-67; col. 6, lines 1-56; col. 7, lines 66-67; col. 8, lines 1-40; col. 9, lines 8-61; col. 10, lines 12-58).
However, the teachings of Tsai fail to specifically disclose the strands are copper strands, and the epoxy resin is a colloid.
Chen teaches a light assembly of a string light (string light 100; see Figs. 1-1A; Abstract; par. [0028]) comprising a first wire and a second wire, each of the first wire and the second wire comprising exposed copper strands (a parallel pair of positive wire 1 and negative wire 2, which comprise bulb welding positions 10 in the form of positive wire bulb welding positions 101 and negative wire bulb welding positions 102 evenly distributed along the two wires to expose the copper wire strands inside the two wires; see Figs .1-1A; para. [0005], [0028]-[0030], [0033], [0041]-[0042], [0045]); a first light emitting diode (LED) chip soldered to the exposed copper strands of the first wire and the second wire (LED chips 3 are soldered to the exposed copper strands of the first wire 1 and second wire 2 at their respective positive wire bulb welding positions 1 and negative wire bulb welding positions 2; see Figs. 1-1A; para. [0028], [0035]-[0036], [0038], [0046]-[0047]); and a colloid encapsulating the first LED chip soldered to the first wire and the second wire (the entire first LED chip 3, including the points where its electrodes are soldered to the first and second wires 1 and 2, is encapsulated by a high-transmission epoxy resin colloid 4; see Figs. 1-1A; para. [0028], [0047]).
Therefore, in view of Chen, it would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art before the effective filing date of the claimed invention to modify the light assembly of Tsai by forming the wire strands of each of the first and second wires as copper strands, since it has been held by the courts that selection of a prior art material on the basis of its suitability for its intended purpose is within the level of ordinary skill. See In re Leshing, 125 USPQ 416 (CCPA 1960) and Sinclair & Carroll Co. v. Interchemical Corp., 65 USPQ 297 (1945). One would have been motivated to modify the known light assembly of Tsai by forming the wire strands of each of the first and second wires as copper strands, as taught by Chen, in order to improve the overall flexibility of the wires and electrical conductivity of the wires.
Further, in view of Chen, it would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art before the effective filing date of the claimed invention to modify the light assembly of Tsai by forming the epoxy resin encapsulating the first LED chips as a colloid, See In re Leshing, 125 USPQ 416 (CCPA 1960) and Sinclair & Carroll Co. v. Interchemical Corp., 65 USPQ 297 (1945). One would have been motivated to modify the known light assembly of Tsai by forming the epoxy resin encapsulating the first LED chips as a colloid, as taught by Chen, in order to ensure a full 360 degrees of transmission from each LED chip and maximize the light transmission through the encapsulant (see Chen, par. [0047] for the motivation).
Regarding claim 2, Tsai teaches the light assembly further comprising a rear plug placed in a space between the first wire and the second wire where the first wire and second wire diverge (spacer plug 108; see Figs. 1A-1F, 7A-8; col. 6, lines 30-49; col. 7, lines 8-44; , 58-65; col. 8, lines 15-40; col. 13, lines 15-67; col. 15, lines 20-67).
However, regarding claim 3, the teachings of Tsai as modified fail to disclose or fairly suggest the light assembly further comprising a second LED chip soldered to the exposed copper strands of the first wire and the second wire.
It would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art before the effective filing date of the claimed invention to further modify the light assembly of Tsai by soldering a second LED chip to the exposed copper strands of the first wire and the second wire, since it has been held that mere duplication of essential working parts of a device involves only routine skill in the art.  St. Regis Paper Co. v. Bemis Co., 193 USPQ 8. In this case, further modifying the known light assembly of Tsai by soldering a second LED chip to the exposed copper strands of the first wire and the second wire would have flown naturally to one of ordinary skill in the art as necessitated by the particular design requirements of a given application, in order to increase the amount of light emitted by each light assembly.
Regarding claim 4, Tsai teaches wherein the string light comprises a plurality of light assemblies (the light string 120 comprises a plurality of light assemblies 100; see Fig. 9; col. 16, lines 8-35).
Regarding claim 5, Tsai as modified teaches wherein the first LED chip comprises an anode and a cathode (the first LED chip 110 includes a first contact 110A functioning as an anode connector of the LED and a second contact 110B functioning as a cathode connector of the LED, which are each soldered to the exposed strands of the first and second wires 112, 114; see Figs. 1A-1F, 2; col. 6, lines 57-67; col. 7, lines 1-44; col. 10, lines 31-50; col. 14, lines 19-51); and wherein the anode is soldered to the exposed copper strand of the first wire and the cathode is soldered to the exposed copper strand of the second wire (see Figs. 1A-1F, 2; col. 6, lines 57-67; col. 7, lines 1-44; col. 10, lines 31-50; col. 14, lines 19-51).
Regarding claim 6, Tsai teaches wherein the decorative shell is in the shape of one of a mini light bulb, round globe, snowflake, and pentagram (the decorative shell 104 can have a generally frusto-conical shape as a miniature light bulb and other suitable shapes such as for decorative, functional, or other purposes; see Figs. 1A-1F, 2, 8-9; col. 4, lines 61-67; col. 5, lines 1-9).
Regarding claim 7, Tsai teaches a method of making a light assembly of a string light (light assembly 100 of a light string 120 of connected light assemblies; see Figs. 1A-9; Abstract; col. 4, lines 23-60; col. 6, lines 50-56; col. 7, lines 8-20, 45-57; col. 15, lines 58-67; col. 16, lines 1-35), the method comprising providing a first wire and a second wire (first conductive lead wire 112 and second conductive lead wire 114 each have exposed conductors at their ends; see Figs. 1A-1F, 2, 8-9; col. 6, lines 50-67; col. 7, lines 1-65); stripping an end of each of the first wire and the second wire of insulation to expose a portion of strands of each of the first wire and the second wire (first conductive lead wire 112 and second conductive lead wire 114 each have exposed conductors at their ends; see Figs. 1A-1F, 2, 8-9; col. 6, lines 50-67; col. 7, lines 1-65); soldering a first LED chip to the first wire and the second wire (a light emitting source 110 which comprises a light emitter 110C in the form of an LED is soldered to the exposed conductive strands of the first wire 112 and the second wire 114; see Figs. 1A-1F, 2, 8-9; col. 6, lines 50-67; col. 7, lines 1-65; col. 10, lines 20-50); encapsulating the first LED chip with an epoxy resin (a filler 116 such as epoxy resin or similar material is deposited in a light cap 104 and positioned over the first LED 110 to encapsulate the LED and its solder connections to the first and second wires 112, 114; see Figs. 1A-1F, 2; 8-9; col. 7, lines 66-67; col. 8, lines 1-47; col. 10, lines 12-58); attaching a light head to the first wire and the second wire (a housing 106 is connected to the first wire 112 and the second wire 114; see Figs. 1A-6C, 8-9; col. 4, lines 47-52; col. 5, lines 36-67; col. 6, lines 13-56; col. 7, lines 8-31, 66-67; col. 8, lines 1-40, 63-67; col. 10, lines 12-67); and securing a decorative shell on the light head, wherein the decorative shell and light head enclose the epoxy resin encapsulating the first LED chip (light cap 104 is secured onto the light head 106 and encloses the epoxy resin 116 encapsulating the first LED chip 110 therein; see Figs. 1A-1F, 2, 8-9; col. 4, lines 47-67; col. 5, lines 1-35, 59-67; col. 6, lines 1-56; col. 7, lines 66-67; col. 8, lines 1-40; col. 9, lines 8-61; col. 10, lines 12-58).
However, the teachings of Tsai fail to specifically disclose the strands are copper strands, and the epoxy resin is a colloid.
Chen teaches a method of making a light assembly of a string light (string light 100; see Figs. 1-1A; Abstract; par. [0028]), the method comprising providing a first wire and a second wire, and stripping portions of each of the first wire and second wire of insulation to expose a portion of copper strands of each of the first wire and the second wire (a parallel pair of positive wire 1 and negative wire 2, which comprise bulb welding positions 10 in the form of positive wire bulb welding positions 101 and negative wire bulb welding positions 102 evenly distributed along the two wires to expose the copper wire strands inside the two wires; see Figs .1-1A; para. [0005], [0028]-[0030], [0033], [0041]-[0042], [0045]); soldering a first LED chip to the first wire and the second wire (LED chips 3 are soldered to the exposed copper strands of the first wire 1 and second wire 2 at their respective positive wire bulb welding positions 1 and negative wire bulb welding positions 2; see Figs. 1-1A; para. [0028], [0035]-[0036], [0038], [0046]-[0047]); and encapsulating the first LED chip with a colloid (the entire first LED chip 3, including the points where its electrodes are soldered to the first and second wires 1 and 2, is encapsulated by a high-transmission epoxy resin colloid 4; see Figs. 1-1A; para. [0028], [0047]).
Therefore, in view of Chen, it would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art before the effective filing date of the claimed invention to modify the method of making a light assembly of Tsai by forming the wire strands of each of the first and second wires as copper strands, since it has been held by the courts that selection of a prior art material on the basis of its suitability for its intended purpose is within the level of ordinary skill. See In re Leshing, 125 USPQ 416 (CCPA 1960) and Sinclair & Carroll Co. v. Interchemical Corp., 65 USPQ 297 (1945). One would have been motivated to modify the known method of Tsai by forming the wire strands of each of the first and second wires as copper strands, as taught by Chen, in order to improve the overall flexibility of the wires and electrical conductivity of the wires.
Further, in view of Chen, it would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art before the effective filing date of the claimed invention to modify the method of making a light assembly of Tsai by forming the epoxy resin encapsulating the first LED chips as a colloid, See In re Leshing, 125 USPQ 416 (CCPA 1960) and Sinclair & Carroll Co. v. Interchemical Corp., 65 USPQ 297 (1945). One would have been motivated to modify the known method of Tsai by forming the epoxy resin encapsulating the first LED chips as a colloid, as taught by Chen, in order to ensure a full 360 degrees of transmission from each LED chip and maximize the light transmission through the encapsulant (see Chen, par. [0047] for the motivation).
Regarding claim 8, Tsai teaches the method further comprising placing a rear plug in a space between the first wire and the second wire where the first wire and the second wire diverge (spacer plug 108; see Figs. 1A-1F, 7A-8; col. 6, lines 30-49; col. 7, lines 8-44; , 58-65; col. 8, lines 15-40; col. 13, lines 15-67; col. 15, lines 20-67).
Regarding claim 9, Tsai as modified teaches the method wherein soldering the first wire and the second wire comprises soldering an anode of the first LED chip to the exposed copper strands of the first wire and soldering a cathode of the first LED chip to the exposed copper strands of the second wire (the first LED chip 110 includes a first contact 110A functioning as an anode connector of the LED and a second contact 110B functioning as a cathode connector of the LED, which are each soldered to the exposed strands of the first and second wires 112, 114; see Figs. 1A-1F, 2; col. 6, lines 57-67; col. 7, lines 1-44; col. 10, lines 31-50; col. 14, lines 19-51).
Regarding claim 10, Tsai teaches the method wherein the light head is assembled or made by foam injection (the entire light head (housing 106) can be injection molded or otherwise machined (i.e., assembled); see Figs. 1A-1G, 3-6C, 8-11D,  col. 12, lines 30-34).
Regarding claim 11, Tsai as modified teaches the method wherein the colloid is formed over the first LED chip using one of injection molding, casting, and foam injection (the epoxy resin 116 is injected into the decorative shell (light cap 104) to secure the decorative shell to the light head 106 and encapsulate the first LED chip 110 and its solder connections to the first and second wires 112, 114; see Figs. 1A-1F, 2; col. 7, lines 66-67; col. 8, lines 1-40).
However, regarding claim 12, the teachings of Tsai as modified fail to disclose or fairly suggest the method further comprises soldering a second LED chip to the exposed copper strands of the first wire and the second wire.
It would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art before the effective filing date of the claimed invention to further modify the method of making a light assembly of Tsai by soldering a second LED chip to the exposed copper strands of the first wire and the second wire, since it has been held that mere duplication of essential working parts of a device involves only routine skill in the art.  St. Regis Paper Co. v. Bemis Co., 193 USPQ 8. In this case, further modifying the known method of Tsai by soldering a second LED chip to the exposed copper strands of the first wire and the second wire would have flown naturally to one of ordinary skill in the art as necessitated by the particular design requirements of a given application, in order to increase the amount of light emitted by each light assembly.
Conclusion
The prior art made of record and not relied upon is considered pertinent to applicant's disclosure. Tsai (US 11,499,700), Chen (US 10,393,351), Yu (US 8,083,393), and Tsai (US 7,740,503) all disclose light assemblies of light strings comprising first and second wires having an LED electrically connected to the wires by solder or other conventional methods and enclosed by at least a light head and a decorative shell.
